title: L'Arrestation d'Arsène Lupin
author: Maurice Leblanc
blurb: A transatlantic liner, a wireless telegram, and a gentleman-thief hiding somewhere among the first-class passengers.

p: What a strange voyage! And yet it had begun so well.
The liner La Provence was a fast, comfortable ship, and the passengers who had boarded at Le Havre formed a small, elegant society.
There were about a hundred of us in first class: businessmen, artists, a few young women going to join their families in America, and old ladies who spent their days playing cards.
In the evening, we dined together in the big dining room, then we danced, or else we strolled on deck under the stars.
It was like a small floating town, where everybody knew each other after two days.
For a week, we were going to live together, far from the world, without news from land.
At least, that is what we thought.
For some time now, the big ships had had an extraordinary invention: the wireless telegraph, thanks to which you could receive messages in the middle of the sea.
On the second day, five hundred miles from the French coast, on a stormy afternoon, the telegraph brought us this message:
'Arsène Lupin on board, first class, blond hair, wound on right forearm, travelling alone, under the name R...'
At that very moment, a violent clap of thunder broke out, and the rest of the message never arrived.
Of the name under which Arsène Lupin was hiding, we knew only the first letter.
It is impossible to describe the excitement that took hold of the passengers.
Arsène Lupin! The gentleman-burglar whose exploits all the newspapers had been reporting for months!
This mysterious man stole countesses' jewels and millionaires' paintings, but he never went after the poor.
People said he could take on any face: one day he was a chauffeur; the next, he became a baron or a doctor.

People said that one day he had stolen a painting from a baron's château, and that in its place he had left a perfect copy, with a little card: 'Arsène Lupin will come back when the furniture is genuine.'
Old Inspector Ganimard, who had been chasing him for years, had sworn that he would arrest him one day.
And this famous thief was there, among us, in the small closed world of our boat!
'Admit that it's fun,' Miss Nelly Underdown said to me that evening, on deck. 'I find it delightful.'
Miss Nelly was a young American woman, beautiful, cheerful and very rich.
Her father, a Chicago banker, was waiting for her in New York.
She was travelling with a friend, Lady Jerland, who watched over her like a mother.
From the very first day, I had done my best to please her, and I had the impression that she didn't find me unpleasant.
But I had a rival: a certain Mr Rozaine, a tall, blond, elegant and slightly pretentious young man, who never left her side.
'You who are so clever, Monsieur d'Andrézy,' Miss Nelly went on, 'you should unmask Arsène Lupin. That would be quite a feat!'
'If I unmasked him, what would you give me?'
She laughed. 'I don't know... Perhaps my friendship.'
'Then it's settled: I shall lead the investigation.
Let's start with the simplest part. Lupin is blond, he travels alone, and his name begins with an R. All we need to do is look at the passenger list.'
'You talk like a real detective!' she said, laughing.
If she had known how well placed I was to lead this investigation...
The next morning, we asked the captain for the passenger list, and we studied it together, Miss Nelly and I.
There were only five men whose name began with an R, and three of them were travelling with their families.
That left two: the Marquis de Raverdan, who was at least sixty, and... Mr Rozaine.
'Rozaine!' cried Miss Nelly. 'He's blond, he travels alone... That would be too good to be true!'
To be quite sure, we went to observe the Marquis de Raverdan at breakfast.
He was eating a boiled egg extraordinarily slowly, and he fell asleep twice before the end of the meal.
'If that's Arsène Lupin,' whispered Miss Nelly, 'then he's the best actor in the world.'
That left Rozaine, then, and I must admit that the idea did not displease me.
Yet we needed to have proof.
'And the wound on the arm?' I said. 'If Rozaine is Lupin, he must have a scar on his right forearm.'
But Rozaine, who had heard about our suspicions, came to see us himself, smiling.
He rolled up his sleeve in front of everyone: his arm was perfectly unmarked.
Then he announced that he was offering a reward of ten thousand francs to whoever unmasked Arsène Lupin.
The passengers applauded him, and Miss Nelly looked disappointed.
Two days later, a scream woke the whole boat.
During the night, someone had got into Lady Jerland's cabin and stolen her jewels.
The strangest thing was that the thief had not taken everything.
He had carefully removed the diamonds, the pearls and the rubies, and he had left the gold settings on the table, the way you leave the stones after eating cherries.
Nobody doubted that the culprit was Arsène Lupin.
It had to be him: who else would have had such nerve?
From then on, every passenger kept an eye on his neighbour.
People locked their cabins, hid their money, and talked of nothing but the invisible thief.
Lady Jerland was crying in the lounge, surrounded by ladies who were trying to comfort her.
'My diamonds!' she kept saying. 'My grandmother's diamonds!'
Miss Nelly was more thoughtful than sad.
She asked me in a low voice: 'How could he get in? The door was locked, I'm sure of it.'
'For a man like Lupin, a lock is no obstacle,' I replied.
That same evening, a man was found lying on the deck, in a dark corner.
He was tied up and gagged, and his head was wrapped in a thick blanket.
When they untied him, they recognised Mr Rozaine.
He was furious and half suffocated.
He explained that he had been attacked from behind during his evening walk.
His wallet had been taken, and in its place a card had been pinned to his jacket.
On this card you could read: 'Arsène Lupin gratefully accepts Mr Rozaine's ten thousand francs.'
The wallet had contained twelve thousand francs; the thief had given back two thousand, out of politeness.
The passengers didn't know whether to laugh or tremble.
One thing was certain, in any case: Rozaine could not be Arsène Lupin.
You don't attack yourself, and you don't steal your own wallet!
But then, who was he? Where was he hiding?
The captain had the ship searched, from the hold to the funnels, without finding anything.
The next day, the captain received a second telegram, shorter than the first:
'Inspector Ganimard on his way to New York. Will arrive before you. Watch the passengers, but do nothing.'
The captain didn't manage to keep the secret for more than an hour, and soon everyone was talking about it.
'Ganimard against Lupin!' the passengers were saying. 'The duel of the century!'
Some were even betting money on the winner.
Miss Nelly, for her part, had had an idea.
'Since Lupin can change his face,' she said to me, 'we must take photos of all the passengers. Ganimard will compare our photos with the police's.'
I thought the idea was excellent, and I lent her my camera.
For a whole day, we went all over the boat, and Miss Nelly took dozens of photos: sailors, ladies, cooks, and even the captain's cat.
Of course, it never occurred to her to photograph me.
In the evening, she gave me back the camera, very proud of herself. 'With this, Lupin doesn't stand a chance!'
I thanked her, and I put the camera away in my cabin with great care.
It already contained things far more precious than photographs.
During the last days of the voyage, a kind of fever took hold of the boat.
People distrusted everyone, even the children, even the servants.
The Marquis de Raverdan, despite his sixty years, was suspected in his turn, which flattered him a great deal.
As for me, I spent all my time with Miss Nelly.
We strolled on deck, we talked about books, music, America and France.
She was very interested in my camera, and I had taught her how to use it.
Sometimes she looked at me strangely, as if she wanted to ask me a question that she didn't dare to ask.
I believe that at that moment, if she had asked me, I would have confessed everything to her.
On the last evening, there was a big ball in the lounge, and I danced with her until midnight.
'Tomorrow we'll be in New York,' she said to me. 'What will you do there?'
'I don't know yet. That will depend on you.'
She blushed, and she didn't answer.
At last, one morning, we caught sight of the American coast, then the Statue of Liberty.
All the passengers rushed onto the deck to watch New York emerge from the mist.
When the boat came to a stop alongside the quay, I immediately noticed an old man waiting at the bottom of the gangway.
He was wearing an old coat, and he was smoking his pipe with the air of someone who is bored.
He had crossed the Atlantic on a faster boat than ours, and he was waiting for us.
'May I?' I said to Miss Nelly, handing her my camera. 'Keep it for a moment, it's in my way.'
She took it without saying anything.
We went down the gangway together, slowly, in the middle of the crowd.
Ganimard was looking at each face, one after the other.
When I reached him, he put his hand on my arm, gently, almost in a friendly way.
I burst out laughing. 'Of course not, my name is Bernard d'Andrézy!'
'Bernard d'Andrézy died three years ago in Macedonia,' Ganimard replied calmly.
He rolled up my sleeve. On my right arm, there was a scar that was still red.
The telegram had told the truth.
As for the R, it was only a mistake by the operator, who had misheard because of the storm.
That mistake had protected me during the whole voyage, and it had very nearly cost poor Rozaine dearly.
She was very pale, and she was still holding my camera.
At that moment, I understood that she knew.
She knew that Lady Jerland's jewels and Rozaine's money were hidden inside that camera, and that I had entrusted it to her so that it wouldn't be found on me.
All she had to do was give it to Ganimard, and I would be done for.
She took a few steps towards the edge of the quay and, with a slow gesture, she let the camera fall into the water, between the quay and the boat.
Then she walked away without looking at me.
I watched her disappear into the crowd, with her pale dress and her blond hair.
Ganimard led me away, and I let him.
I was thinking less about prison than about Miss Nelly.
Had she wanted to save me, or simply to show me her contempt?
But I know one thing: of all the treasures I have stolen in my life, it is the one I lost that day that I regret the most.
As for prison... Ganimard should have known that no prison can hold Arsène Lupin for very long.

a-t-elle: she has (a-t-elle dit / demandé = she said / asked)
air: look, air (avoir l'air = to look, seem)
au: to the, at the, in the
aurais: would have (j'aurais avoué = I would have confessed)
bas: bottom (au bas de = at the foot of)
basse: low (à voix basse = in a low voice)
cartes: cards (jouer aux cartes = to play cards)
cas: case (en tout cas = in any case)
celui: the one (celui que = the one that)
cher: dearly (coûter cher = to cost a lot)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
coque: shell (un œuf à la coque = a boiled egg)
dire: to say (il faut dire = it must be said)
dès: from (dès le premier jour = from the very first day)
découvrais: discovered (si je découvrais = if I unmasked)
emparée: seized (s'emparer de = to take hold of)
fallait: was necessary (il fallait que = had to)
moment-là: that moment (à ce moment-là = at that moment)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
place: place (à sa place = in its place)
pleine: full (en pleine mer = out at sea)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
point: point (à quel point = how, to what extent)
précipités: se précipiter · past participle, m. pl.
précis: precise (à ce moment précis = at that very moment)
question: question
f.
quittait: left (ne quittait pas d'une semelle = never left her side)
restait: remained, was left (il en restait = there were … left)
rire: to laugh; laughter (éclater de rire = to burst out laughing)
route: way (en route pour = on the way to)
semelle: sole (ne pas quitter d'une semelle = never leave someone's side)
simple: simple (le plus simple = the simplest part)
soit: is, be (que ce soit = that it is)
su: known (je ne l'ai jamais su = I never found out)
suffisait: was enough (il lui suffisait de = all she had to do was)
suffit: is enough (il suffit de = all we need is)
tour: turn (à son tour = in his turn)
trouve: find (pour qu'on ne le trouve pas = so that it wouldn't be found)
vole: steals (on se vole = you steal from yourself)
vue: seen (je l'ai vue = I saw her)
